Chapter 04100 BPMPROCESSING

The Clock

Every city needs a clock. Vancouver rides inside its.

Terminal City calls the SkyTrain the Clock. All day it moves above and beneath the streets, closing doors, sounding chimes, crossing itself and pulling away again. Thousands of people use it to get somewhere; almost none notice what else it is doing. The trains do not follow the rhythm of the city. The city follows the trains. A door closes at Commercial–Broadway and, somewhere across town, a light changes. The Clock does not tell Terminal City what time it is. It distributes time. Occasionally it drifts, by a second or two, and the whole city feels late. Then a train passes, the doors close, and the city catches up.

The Lanky One and the Kid wait beneath the SkyTrain with a bag of brushes between them. The first train comes through as the Kid lifts the bag. Across the neighbourhood, the Cyclist looks up from the courtyard pole at almost the same moment.

Almost is enough to be awkward. At the new entrance, the painter starts a small corner stroke and stops. An upstairs song arrives a fraction behind the door chime in the Kid's headphones. The city feels as though two people have started speaking together and neither will stop.

In Terminal City, the SkyTrain is known as the Clock. The trains carry passengers. They also keep far-apart moments close enough to belong to the same now. Usually this looks like a light changing just as someone reaches it, or a song falling neatly under a station chime.

The Kid puts the bag down. The Lanky One waits. When the Kid reaches for it again too soon, the Lanky One raises one finger. The Kid sits back on the heels. There is no reason to argue with a second.

Another train passes. Its doors close at the station. The Kid picks up the bag; the crossing changes; the painter finishes the short mark. Upstairs, music begins beside an open window.

Nobody fixes the train. It has somewhere to be. The two workers carry the brushes toward the courtyard, where the rest of the morning has caught up.

The ruleIf the SkyTrain chime lands exactly on the beat, don't check the time. The Clock already has it.

Terminal City · Storybook v0.9.0 · built 2026-09-12
Terminal City is an original fictional mythology inspired by Vancouver’s geography, weather, wildlife, infrastructure, art, and electronic music. It makes no claim to historical, Indigenous, or religious tradition. Real places are used as settings; the operating system layered on them is invented.
Made by Steve Hiehn, a software developer and electronic musician based in Vancouver, Canada. All music was created using a custom DAW, Signals & Sorcery.
